turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do hope you're not trying to scare him off, Mother. This is ridiculous.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am afraid that 149, Belgrave Square, is a thoroughly respectable address, but I must know more about the family's connections before I can consider you a suitable husband for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't know very much about my family's connections, Lady Bracknell. My father was a clergyman, and I don't think he ever mentioned any... distinguished relatives.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I suppose a clergyman's son may have some connection to a respectable family, but I must know more about your education, your upbringing, and your present circumstances.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I've had quite enough of this, Mother. I'm not a child to be interrogated about my fiancé's family any more than I am about my own.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you, Mr. Worthing, provide me with some tangible evidence of your social standing. A clergyman's son, indeed! I suppose that is a respectable enough profession, but I require more than mere words to convince me of your suitability as a husband for my daughter.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I've never thought of myself as having any great social standing, Lady Bracknell. I've always tried to do what was right and be a good person, rather than trying to impress others with my family connections or wealth.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your... rustic simplicity is quite charming, but it will not suffice to convince me of your suitability as a husband for my daughter. I require a more substantial demonstration of your intellectual and cultural refinement.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't know much about intellectual and cultural refinement, Lady Bracknell. I've always relied on my own simple tastes and values, rather than trying to cultivate a more... elaborate sensibility.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Worthing, that your candor is a trifle disconcerting, but I fear it will not save you from my scrutiny. I require a more substantial account of your family's history and connections, and I warn you, I will not be satisfied with vague assurances or platitudes.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid, Lady Bracknell, that I'm not very knowledgeable about my family's history, as I was raised by my guardian, an uncle, and I've never had much contact with my relatives. I hope you'll forgive me if I seem... unprepared to answer your questions.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I am astonished, Mr. Worthing, that you were not aware of your family's history. I must insist that you provide me with a detailed account of your ancestry, or I fear our conversation will be at an end.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I do think it's quite absurd, Mother, that you're questioning Jack's suitability as a husband when I'm the one who's really at fault for being so obtuse about my own family's history. I'm perfectly aware that I'm not some noble heiress, but I'm perfectly happy with Jack, and I won't let you bully him into feeling unworthy of me.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I've never thought to investigate my family's history in great detail, Lady Bracknell. I've always assumed that it would be a bit... complicated, and that I'd rather focus on building a life with Gwendolen.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to be made to feel ashamed of who I am, Mother. I'm perfectly happy with Jack, and I won't let you bully me into changing my mind.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you do not speak to your mother in such a tone, Miss Gwendolen. A woman of your standing and breeding should learn to address her elders with respect.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm terribly sorry, Lady Bracknell, but I don't think I can provide the kind of detailed account of my ancestry that you're looking for. I'm afraid it's all a bit of a mystery to me, and I'm more interested in building a life with Gwendolen than in trying to uncover my family's history.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'm not going to let you interrogate Jack like a defendant in a court of law, Mother. He's said all he needs to say.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, your reluctance to provide a full account of your family's history is most... distressing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I don't see what all the fuss is about, Lady Bracknell. I'm a simple man, and I've always thought that a person's character is what truly matters, not their family background.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
